endings.text: Soap and candles both, carried home to the log house behind Peck's. The whole list is done, whichever thing stood at the top of it. The armful and the evening are the story's.
Candles at the top of the list, and candles carried home. Tonight the crowded room behind Peck's has light to read and mend by. The bundle and the evening are the story's.
Soap at the top of the list, and soap carried home. The shirts can wait no longer, and now they need not. The cake of soap and the washing day are the story's.
You set out for one thing and carried home the other. It will be wanted soon enough, and the list keeps until next time. The errand and its muddle are the story's.

evidence.locator: 26 Nov 1833 (Vol. I No. 1), p. 3, col. 5, the advertisement headed 'Grocery & Provision Store. B. JONES.' (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1833_11_26#c018). Transcription-mediated reading of a damaged scan.
evidence.text: B. Jones's 'Grocery & Provision Store' advertisement in the first number of the Chicago Democrat says he keeps constantly on hand sugar and most kinds of provisions, for sale at the lowest prices. It gives no street, and a damaged line between may have named more goods.

evidence.reasoning: Andreas lists Jones among the South Water Street district's advertisers; neither he nor the advertisement gives a block, so the structure record grades the coordinate reconstructed and the stop calls the block our placement. The two sources disagree on the initial (B. or H.), so the stop says only Jones.
evidence.text: Jones's store is placed on the south side of South Water Street just east of Wells; the street is the evidence and the block is not.

evidence.locator: 26 Nov 1833 (Vol. I No. 1), p. 3, col. 6, the advertisement headed 'Chicago Soap and Candle Manufactory' (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1833_11_26#c030); the partner's name is lost under a tear in the scan. Transcription-mediated reading.
evidence.text: Daniel Elston & Co.'s 'Chicago Soap and Candle Manufactory' advertisement announces that they have commenced the manufacture of soap and candles, keep an assortment of hard and soft soap, wax and other candles, and pay cash for tallow in any quantity and for good house ashes.

evidence.locator: 2 July 1834, p. 4, col. 1 (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1834_07_02#c007). Transcription-mediated reading.
evidence.text: The same Elston & Co. advertisement was still printed in the Chicago Democrat of 2 July 1834.

evidence.reasoning: The structure record's position is a conjectural proposal that cites no source for the site; the stop therefore says the place is ours and stays an exterior observation from the road. Nothing records a shop counter at the works.
evidence.text: No source gives the works' site: the advertisement and Andreas's summary of it name the firm and the trade and no street. The scene places it on the east bank of the North Branch above the forks.

evidence.reasoning: The advertisement states what the firm bought (tallow, house ashes) and what it sold (soap, candles); the process that joins them is the ordinary one and is the structure record's own inference about the plant, not a description of these works.
evidence.text: Tallow and house ashes are the two inputs of soap making, the ashes leached for lye and boiled with rendered tallow; candles are the same tallow moulded or dipped.

evidence.locator: Chicagology, early street maps gallery, the editorial addendum at the foot of the page: the Thomas Church sentence (accessed 2026-08-11).
evidence.text: An uncredited modern note says the first store building on Lake Street, a two-storey frame structure, was built by Thomas Church. It gives no year, no stock and no address, and this project grades the note as its weakest kind of source.

evidence.reasoning: The note says 'Lake Street' only. The structure record chose an unclaimed stretch and grades the coordinate reconstructed, so the stop claims no front door and nothing sold.
evidence.text: Church's store is placed mid-block on the north side of Lake Street between LaSalle and Clark; the street is attested and the block is not.

evidence.locator: Vol. 1, printed p. 132, boarding-house paragraph; p. 303, Jeremiah Porter biography.
evidence.text: Andreas names Mrs Rufus Brown as keeper of one of the first-class boarding houses, and places Brown's log house as the first building in the rear of Peck's store.

evidence.reasoning: Andreas gives the position only relative to Peck's store. The structure record sets the house directly south of the store's footprint on the same lot line and grades the coordinate reconstructed, so the stop calls the exact spot our placement.
evidence.text: The boarding house is placed directly behind Peck's store at the south-west corner of South Water and LaSalle; its distance behind the store is not documented.

evidence.reasoning: The sentence describes the houses of 1834 as a class, as the structure record and household file quote it; the stop carries it a year forward to one house of that class in a town the June 1835 papers also found crowded, and says 1834.
evidence.text: Andreas says the town's hotels and boarding houses of 1834 'were always full; and full meant three in a bed sometimes, with the floor covered besides'.

The boarder, the list, which item stands at the top of it, the route, the bundle carried home, where it was obtained, the endings, the timing inputs and the Light for the Evening keepsake are invented connective narrative. No sale, price or customer of any shop is documented, and no named person is met.

keepsake.text: A fictional note of a short list and what you carried home from it in July 1835. No real sale, price or customer of any shop is written on it.
keepsake.title: Light for the Evening

legs.note: Over the main river by a bridge and on to the east bank of the North Branch; no particular path is claimed, and the works' site is our placement.
legs.story: The list in your pocket, the river ahead.

legs.note: Back over the river by a bridge to Lake Street; Church's block is not attested.
A block west and round to the rear of Peck's corner at South Water and LaSalle.
legs.story: The last few steps with the bundle.

opening.text: You board in the log house behind Peck's store, and the evenings are long. Make a short list at a grocer's on South Water Street, see from the road what a soap and candle works made, choose what to carry and bring it home by Lake Street. A quiet outing: the errand is invented; the trades are documented.

premise: Make a short list on South Water Street, see from the road what Daniel Elston & Co.'s works made, choose what to carry, and bring it home to a boarding house behind Peck's store.

choices.consequence: The evenings are the point of the errand.
choices.label: Put candles at the top of the list

choices.consequence: Washing day comes before the evenings.
choices.label: Put soap at the top of the list

stops.narrative: Make a short list. What goes at the top?
stops.text: Start at Jones's grocery on South Water Street. His November 1833 notice offered sugar and most kinds of provisions at the lowest prices; whether he kept soap or candles it does not say. Only the street is evidence; the block is our placement.

choices.consequence: A bundle of candles. Where the story's bundle came from is not recorded.
choices.label: Carry candles home

choices.consequence: One cake of soap. No sale at the works is recorded.
choices.label: Carry a cake of hard soap

choices.consequence: A heavier armful, and the whole list in it.
choices.label: Carry some of each

stops.narrative: Tallow and ashes in, soap and light out.
stops.text: Over the river to where we place Daniel Elston & Co.'s works on the North Branch; no source gives the site. Their notice, printed 1833–34, offered hard and soft soap, wax and other candles, and paid cash for tallow and house ashes. No counter is recorded: look from the road.

stops.narrative: Shift the bundle and count what you carry.
stops.text: Back over the river to Lake Street and the two-storey frame store Thomas Church built, said to be the first store building on the street. One undated sentence is all the evidence, and it names no stock, so nothing is bought here.

stops.narrative: A candle goes a long way in a crowded room.
stops.text: Home to the log house behind Peck's store, which Andreas names as Mrs Rufus Brown's, one of the first-class boarding houses; its exact spot is our placement. In 1834, he writes, such houses were always full, three in a bed sometimes.
